Documentation → Releases → 2.1.0

SATOM 2.1.0

Scout now reads Fortinet's upgrade notes and warns you before a firmware push, open change requests can be edited, devices can be put into maintenance with one click, and the API catalog learns what each exact firmware build serves over REST and the CLI.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user

Released: 2026-09-22 · All releases

In short#

2.1.0 is a large release built mostly from operators' requests. It touches four areas:

  • Firmware upgrades — Scout reads Fortinet's upgrade instructions and tells you, on the upgrade page itself, if the version you are about to install has a known reason not to go ahead.
  • Change requests — an open change can now be corrected instead of being cancelled and retyped.
  • The device inventory — one-click maintenance mode, correct online/offline badges, and a visible history of where each server policy was cloned.
  • The API catalog — SATOM compares what an appliance offers through its CLI with what the catalog knows through REST, can grow the catalog from what a device actually serves, and now keeps its evidence per exact firmware build (for example 8.0.5) instead of per release line (8.0).

Operators who upgrade firmware or work with change requests will notice the most. Administrators who maintain the API catalog get a whole new set of tools.

What's new#

Firmware upgrades and release notes#

Scout Advisory: the upgrade instructions as verdicts#

The Upgrade advisor tab of the Release Notes window now opens with a Scout Advisory, placed above the list of fixed bugs because a blocking prerequisite decides whether your maintenance window can happen at all.

Each finding gives a severity, an instruction in plain words, and Fortinet's original sentence word for word. Scout recognises:

  • mandatory intermediate versions (an upgrade that needs two steps);
  • free disk space requirements;
  • the disk repartitioning required when coming from very old versions;
  • how an HA cluster behaves during the upgrade;
  • backups that will not restore after the upgrade;
  • virtual-machine licences that must be validated again;
  • three known traps when downgrading.

Anything else Fortinet marked as Caution or Warning is passed through as well, so vendor warnings no rule understands still reach you.

A few rules keep the advisory honest:

  • Missing information is never a green light. If the release notes for a version were never collected, the result is unknown, never clear, and the advisory lists what is missing. It also tells you when notes were collected before a section existed and a new scan would help.
  • Upgrades and downgrades are treated separately. An upgrade advisory never quotes the downgrade instructions, and the reverse.
  • Every advisory names the rule set that produced it, so an archived advisory can be traced back later.

Scout reviews the target firmware on the upgrade page#

At an operator's request, the advisory now also appears next to the firmware picker on the device's upgrade page, with an opt-in checkbox. It reviews the image you have selected and refreshes when you pick another one. It appears for a dry run as well as a real upgrade, because the dry run is where you decide.

  • When the verdict is a blocker or a caution, it is saved with the upgrade job and written to the audit log, so you can later prove the warning was shown.
  • Scout advises; it does not stop the upgrade. Change control decides whether an upgrade may run. A gap in SATOM's collected notes should never look like a refusal by Fortinet.
  • Nothing that did not run looks clean. If Scout is switched off, was not asked, does not support the product, cannot read the running version or cannot read its notes, it says unavailable and gives the reason.

As an example, moving a FortiWeb from 7.6.8 to 8.0.7 returns a blocker, quoting Fortinet's advice not to upgrade virtual machines to 8.0.7, while the same move to 8.0.5 returns a caution.

Scout catches warnings it used to miss#

Scout now recognises two kinds of warning it previously could not see:

  • Warnings written in a different page style. Fortinet changed how its release notes are laid out, and the old reader missed every marked warning in the new style. Warnings are now read in both styles and shown with the label Fortinet used (for example Warning), rather than being renamed.
  • Warnings about the destination version itself, such as "do not upgrade to this version if you have more than a certain number of server policies". These apply whatever version you start from. They now appear first, because "do not do this upgrade" matters more than "this upgrade needs two steps".

SATOM also now checks that every collected version yields at least some warnings; a version with none means the reader no longer matches Fortinet's pages, not that the release is quiet.

Scout can be switched off#

A new Settings → Scout → Availability switch, also shown beside the advisory in the Release Notes window, turns Scout off for the whole site. Both switches control the same setting. When Scout is off, its pages answer that the service is unavailable (also for bookmarks and direct links), and its menu entry stays visible but greyed out with the reason.

More upgrade instructions are collected#

Five pages that sit beside Upgrading from previous releases in Fortinet's documentation are now collected and searchable in the Notes tab:

  • Repartitioning the hard disk
  • Upgrading an HA cluster
  • Downgrading to a previous release
  • Image checksums
  • FortiWeb-VM license validation

Before, every blocking prerequisite on those pages was missing from SATOM.

Discover versions before you scan#

The release-notes scan panel has a new Discover versions step. It reads which versions Fortinet actually publishes, marks the ones SATOM already holds, and ticks the rest. Only the versions you tick are scanned, exactly as ticked, so you can now pick a single maintenance release such as 8.0.7.

The version picker is now laid out as one column per release line:

  • each column has a tick that selects or clears the whole line, shown as half-ticked when only part of it is selected, plus a count of what is selected in it;
  • the versions SATOM already holds carry a check mark, explained by a legend, and the others stay unmarked;
  • on narrower windows the columns wrap neatly without cutting any off.

Reload corpus#

A new Reload corpus button re-reads the collected release notes and tells you where they came from and how old they are. Use it when another node or a scan in progress has just produced newer notes.

Change requests#

Edit an open change request#

At an operator's request, an open change request can now be edited. Before, a change saved without a maintenance window could never run, and the only fix was to cancel it and type it again.

  • You can change: title, reason, rollback plan, owner, who is notified, risk, document language, approval mode and the maintenance window.
  • You cannot change: the action and the devices. The service inventory, pre-flight evidence and any document already circulated describe exactly those devices doing exactly that action. To change them, raise a new change.
  • Closed changes cannot be edited at all; the form does not even open.
  • An approval covers what was approved. Changing the window, the risk or the approval mode sends the change back to draft, clears the approval (including an external approver's record) and disables the action scheduled for the old window. Changing any other field keeps the approval.
  • Raising and editing a change use the same rule for a valid window, so a window that ends before it starts is refused in both places.

You need the same permission as for other change-request management.

Devices and server policies#

Maintenance mode with one click#

At an operator's request, you can now put a device into maintenance mode, or take it out, directly:

  • from its row in the appliance inventory table;
  • from the header of the device's own page, for every product type, including FortiAuthenticator and FortiAnalyzer.

Before, this needed the full edit form. Maintenance mode is more than a label: it hides the device from operators and read-only users and stops scheduled probes and metric collection. So:

  • you need the same permissions as in the edit form: permission to edit the device and permission to see devices in maintenance;
  • entering maintenance asks you to confirm; leaving it does not, because leaving is the undo;
  • leaving maintenance restarts monitoring for the device, just as the edit form does;
  • the button sets the state you see, so a stale browser tab or a colleague clicking at the same time cannot flip it the wrong way.

See where a server policy was cloned#

At an operator's request, a small flag now appears beside a server policy's name when that policy has been cloned or migrated. It shows the number of copies that actually landed, and turns red when every attempt failed. Hover over it, or focus it, to see the full history: the action, the destination device (with its name at the time), the name the copy landed under, the result, the time and the user.

  • A migration is shown as a move, not as a clone, because the original was disabled.
  • Failed attempts are kept with their reason, but are not counted as copies.
  • The history survives the destination device being retired.

API catalog, CLI coverage and discovery#

These tools are for administrators who maintain SATOM's API catalog. They are read-only towards appliances: nothing here changes a device's configuration.

What the CLI has that the catalog does not#

At an operator's request, the API page of every ADOM (the FortiWeb API-Registry Explorer and the FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator API pages) gains a CLI coverage section. It compares the CLI configuration captured from an appliance with the REST catalog and sorts the results into:

  • CLI only — configuration the CLI shows and the catalog does not know, split into tables that hold configuration on that device and tables that are empty there. On a lab FortiWeb this found 55 such blocks, such as automation stitches and webhooks, credential-stuffing checks and cloud logging; on a lab FortiADC it found 84, including routing (BGP and OSPF) settings.
  • Same object, different path — the CLI and REST name it differently.
  • In the catalog, but not in this capture — not proof it is missing: an empty configuration table simply does not appear in the capture.
  • Cannot have a CLI block — status and monitoring readouts, left out of every count.

From a CLI-only row you can open that block in the stored capture, or run a read-only show command against a live appliance right now.

FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator show a short explanation instead of an empty comparison, because neither has a CLI configuration SATOM can compare.

Some safeguards:

  • A capture that does not say which firmware it came from is never compared, and a capture that appears cut short is flagged above the counts.
  • The configuration text itself is shown only to users with backup permission. Passwords, keys and certificates are hidden; setting names stay visible.

Add a CLI-only element to the catalog#

A CLI-only row can be turned into a catalog entry, but its REST path cannot be worked out for certain. SATOM tries every likely path (up to eight, and it says when it stopped there), asks an appliance, and shows what the device answered: served, absent or error. Only a path the appliance actually served can be registered, through the normal catalog editor. If none is served, the page says so: the element really is CLI-only on that firmware.

The sweep can capture the CLI in the same pass#

The rediscovery sweep can now also take a CLI configuration capture, as a separate, optional third step. The REST snapshot is saved first, so a slow or failed SSH connection can never cost you a sweep that already succeeded. A CLI capture takes up to five minutes and stores a copy of the device configuration, which is why it is never done unless asked.

When no capture is taken, the reason is always stated:

  • it was not requested;
  • the product has no CLI configuration capture (FortiAnalyzer, FortiAuthenticator);
  • you do not have permission to write to the configuration vault;
  • the appliance is in maintenance mode;
  • a usable capture less than 24 hours old already exists.

An encrypted capture, one from another appliance, or one of unknown age does not count as "usable", so it never prevents a new capture. A skipped capture and a failed capture are always reported separately.

Which transport serves each endpoint#

At an operator's request, the API versions page, the API pages and the Structure page now show, for every endpoint, whether it is served by the API, the CLI or both:

  • API + CLI — both have it;
  • API + CLI · other path — both have it, named differently;
  • API only — a readout that cannot exist in the CLI;
  • API · no CLI block here — in the catalog, not in this capture (not proof the CLI lacks it).

When there is no capture to compare, the column shows a dash with the reason in its tooltip, rather than a badge that could be mistaken for a result. On the API versions page the comparison is made per firmware line, and endpoint rows are now listed rather than only counted. FortiADC gets the same badges; FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator do not, for the reason above. The API pages also now name the firmware build their badges are based on.

Search and test on every endpoint list#

The Structure page, the API versions page and the API pages all have a filter box and two test buttons per row: test over REST and test over the CLI. They are kept separate on purpose, because the two can disagree, and that disagreement is what these pages are for.

CLI-only elements on the Structure page#

At an operator's request, the Structure page now lists configuration blocks that exist only in the CLI, as their own branch of the tree. Each shows its CLI path, whether it holds configuration on the captured device, a filter and a per-row show test. They are not attached under a server policy, because no field links them there and guessing a link would produce a tree the appliance rejects.

The page also lists the clone gap: blocks that hold configuration but would be missing from a cloned device, because cloning works through REST. To make one clonable, register a REST path the appliance serves, then declare its parent field in the structure overrides.

Grow the catalog with a discovery run#

Until now the catalog could effectively only shrink: SATOM asks a device for the endpoints the catalog names, so it never discovered new ones. The new discovery run takes the CLI-only blocks, works out candidate REST paths, asks the appliance and offers for registration only the paths it served.

  • Each block that is not registered ends as absent (the device said no), error (SATOM could not ask) or not probed (the run's budget ran out first). "Not probed" never means "no REST path exists".
  • A run stays within a request budget (240 by default), stops asking about a block as soon as one candidate is served, and reports how many requests it actually made.
  • Load both refreshes the REST catalog and the CLI capture in one action, so the comparison describes the same device at the same moment. If you lack vault permission, the CLI half is skipped and the reason is shown.
  • When you register, SATOM asks the device again, so it never trusts a list that may have changed since the run.

One appliance, and its firmware. The discovery card now has a single appliance selector. Asking a different appliance, for example a lab twin of a production box, is still possible behind an expandable option, so it is a deliberate choice rather than a mistake. The card always shows which capture, which firmware line and which date the comparison is based on. Before asking anything, the run reads the appliance's running firmware, saves it, and compares it with the firmware of the capture: same, different or unknown. A mismatch is a warning, never a block, and the verdict is saved in the audit log with the run.

A discovery run is a job. The run now works in the background, with live progress, a Stop button, a notification and the bell when it finishes, and an entry in the Job Manager. Its findings are saved with the job, so closing the tab no longer throws away the results. Starting a second run against the same appliance reconnects you to the one already running. The Load both step also shows its progress by phase (REST sweep, deep capture, CLI capture) and reports the CLI result as captured (with its size), skipped (with the reason) or failed (with the error).

Where to find it. The discovery card first moved to the top of the FortiWeb and FortiADC API pages, open by default. Later in this release it moved to the API versions page, where each row is a firmware build: starting a run from a row limits the capture, the appliances offered and the audit entry to that build. The API pages keep a note pointing to its new place.

Evidence per exact firmware build#

At an operator's request, SATOM now records which endpoints a device serves per exact build (8.0.4, 8.0.7) rather than per release line (8.0). Two builds of the same line can differ, and treating them as one could make the compatibility check answer compatible for a build that does not serve an endpoint, right before a write to a production appliance.

  • Every sweep is kept per firmware build, with no limit, so upgrading a device no longer erases the evidence about its previous build. Existing snapshots are filed under their build automatically.
  • A release line is still shown, as a summary that lists the builds it combines, flags itself when they differ, and marks endpoints only some builds serve as partial.
  • A build with no evidence is shown as unmeasured, with the line's answer beside it, clearly labelled.
  • "8.0" (line known, build unknown) is never treated as 8.0.0.
  • Builds become known automatically from uploaded firmware images and from the firmware your devices run, and can also be declared by hand. A known build with no evidence yet shows declared · unmeasured.
  • CLI captures carry their build, and a capture from another build is never used in its place.

Structure by firmware build#

The Structure page has a new firmware selector and a Serves it? column with three answers: served, absent on this build and unmeasured. With no firmware chosen, the column stays empty. The tree itself stays the same for every build, because it is a hand-made map rather than a measurement.

What changes for you#

  • The Release Notes window no longer has Publish to git or Sync from git. Neither had worked for weeks, and the sync could be triggered by a read-only account. Reload corpus replaces them. Release notes are shared between nodes by replication.
  • A release-notes scan only covers the versions you ticked. A request that combines contradictory choices is refused instead of guessing.
  • A status check no longer counts as an edit. The time a device was last changed now really means the last configuration change, not the last time its status was polled.
  • A device's firmware read during a sweep now carries the time it was observed, so you can tell how fresh it is.
  • Buttons always keep their label on one line, everywhere in SATOM.

Fixed#

Devices

  • Every status badge showed "offline" while the appliances were answering. For about three and a half weeks the whole inventory could be shown as offline, and every view that reads that status (tables, reports, analysis, the advisor and the API) inherited the wrong value. Badges now show the real state. When a status check does fail, the log names the appliance.

Firmware and release notes

  • A release whose notes Fortinet published in a new page layout was reported as having no release notes, and scans still finished green. Both layouts are now read. A published page SATOM cannot read is now reported as unreadable, with a warning in the bell, instead of being treated as unpublished, and a genuinely empty issues page is recognised as such.
  • The scan ignored the versions you typed: with one line typed and All discovered ticked, it collected every version, and a single maintenance release could not be entered at all. The new Discover step replaces this.
  • If Discover finds no versions, you now get an error rather than an empty picker.
  • After an update, the Release Notes window could show the previous version of itself for up to a day, which looked like the fix had not been installed. It now always loads the current version.

Change requests and the upgrade flow

  • The Cancel CR button on a change request wrapped onto three lines. It is now one line, and no other button can wrap.
  • In stage 2 of the Upgrade flow, a refused change lost everything you had typed, the proposed wording from Administration → Change Types was not shown, and the Or split the same selection into waves block and the Edit this wording link were missing. Stage 2 again keeps your text and its automatic-field marks after a refusal, shows the wording and offers waves.

API catalog and discovery

  • On the API pages, the Structure page and the API versions page, the buttons of the new tools (What would it cost?, Run discovery, Register selected, the filter boxes and the per-row test buttons) did nothing, because the browser blocked them. They now work.
  • A sweep interrupted by a service restart could show "running" forever, in one case at 71 % for 74 days. It now shows interrupted; a sweep that crashes shows failed with the error; and on an HA pair a node never judges the other node's sweeps.
  • Saving a catalog entry from the FortiWeb page could overwrite a FortiADC entry, and a newly registered FortiADC endpoint could appear in the catalog but not in the menu. Both are fixed.
  • The CLI capture skipped note on the discovery card is shown as a grey badge again instead of plain text.

Before you upgrade#

  • Publish to git and Sync from git are removed from the Release Notes window. Use Reload corpus instead.
  • The clone history flag starts empty. It only shows clones and migrations made after this upgrade.
  • An API comparison saved by an older version is shown as it is, and flagged. SATOM does not rebuild it automatically, because rebuilding would drop evidence from devices that have since been removed. Questions about a specific build are refused against it, with the reason.
  • Review Settings → Scout → Availability if you want Scout off on your site.

Under the hood#

  • The discovery run builds its plan in the page request, in your ADOM, and only the questions to the device run in the background, so a background task can never answer about the wrong ADOM.
  • All writes to the API catalog now go through a single path, so the FortiWeb and FortiADC editors can no longer drift apart.
  • Release notes are loaded from one place only, so two parts of SATOM cannot read them from different folders.
  • SATOM's own tests can no longer overwrite a node's live API comparison data.
